absolute monarch: A king who has all the power by himself: he makes the laws, judges and commands the army, without having to answer to anyone.
clergy: All the people who work for the Church: bishops, priests, monks and nuns. They were the First Estate of the kingdom.
nobility: The group of nobles: families with a title (duke, count, marquis...) and special rights passed down from parents to children. They were the Second Estate.
privilege: An advantage kept for only some people. Before the Revolution, nobles and clergy paid very few taxes: that was a privilege.
bourgeoisie: The rich and educated members of the Third Estate who lived in towns: bankers, merchants, lawyers, doctors. One of them is called a bourgeois.
third estate: The third group of society before 1789: everyone who was neither a noble nor a member of the clergy, which means 98% of the French.
enlightenment philosophers: 18th-century writers and thinkers, like Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau and Diderot, who wanted to enlighten people through reason and knowledge.
reason: The ability to think, work things out and understand for yourself, instead of believing what you are told without checking.
separation of powers: The idea that different people should have the power to make laws, the power to carry them out and the power to judge, so that nobody becomes a tyrant.
declaration of independence: The text adopted on 4 July 1776 in which the thirteen British colonies in America announced that they no longer belonged to the King of England.
constitution: A country's most important text. It sets the rules of power: who makes the laws, who governs, how leaders are chosen, and what rights citizens have.
deficit: When you spend more money than you earn. To cover the difference, you have to borrow, and so you get into debt.
affair of the diamond necklace: A swindle in 1785 involving a very expensive diamond necklace. Queen Marie Antoinette was innocent, but the scandal damaged her reputation.
parlement: Before the Revolution, a parlement was not an elected assembly: it was a high court, run by noble judges, which could protest against the king's laws.
riot: A sudden, often violent uprising by a group of angry people, for example because of the price of bread.
pamphlet: A short booklet, often funny or very critical, written to attack an idea, a person or a government.
nation: All the people of a country who share a history and want to live together. For the revolutionaries, it was the nation, not the king, that held power.
cahiers de doléances: The "books of grievances" written in spring 1789 all over France, in which people wrote down their complaints and wishes for the Estates-General.
estates-general: A great assembly of representatives of the three estates (clergy, nobility, Third Estate), which the king rarely called, mostly to talk about taxes.
national assembly: The assembly of representatives of the whole nation. It was born on 17 June 1789. Today, French deputies still sit in the National Assembly.
real tennis: A ball game that was very popular long ago, called jeu de paume in French. Players first hit the ball with their hand, then with a racket. It is the ancestor of tennis.
arbitrary: Depending only on what someone wants, without any rule or law. Putting someone in prison without a trial is arbitrary.
national holiday: The day when a country celebrates its history. In France, it is 14 July.
great fear: A wave of panic that swept through the French countryside in summer 1789: peasants believed that brigands sent by the nobles were coming to destroy their crops.
émigré: A French word for someone who leaves their country to live elsewhere. During the Revolution, it mainly means the nobles who fled France.
national guard: A militia of volunteer citizens created in 1789 to keep order and defend the Revolution. Lafayette was its first leader.
cockade: A round badge made of pleated ribbon, pinned to a hat. The blue, white and red cockade showed that you supported the Revolution.
feudal: Coming from the Middle Ages, the time of lords and vassals. Feudal dues forced peasants to pay and work for their lord.
sovereignty: The highest power, the one that has the final say. With the Revolution, sovereignty passed from the king to the nation.
département: One of the areas France was divided into in 1790. You were supposed to be able to ride from anywhere to its main town in one day. Today there are 101.
commune: The smallest division of French territory, matching a town or village, with its own mayor and council.
national properties: The land and buildings taken from the Church (and later from émigré nobles) by the Revolution, then sold to pay off the state's debts.
civil constitution of the clergy: The 1790 law that reorganised the Church in France: priests and bishops were elected and paid by the state, and had to swear loyalty to the Constitution.
refractory priest: A priest who refused to swear the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, because the Pope had condemned it.
republic: A system without a king, where power belongs to the people and their elected representatives. The word comes from the Latin res publica, "the public thing".
club: During the Revolution, a meeting place where people discussed politics, like the Jacobin Club or the Cordeliers Club.
petition: A text signed by many people to ask their leaders for something.
declaration of the rights of woman and o: The text written by Olympe de Gouges in 1791 to demand that women have the same rights as men.
constitutional monarchy: A system with a king, but whose powers are limited by a constitution and shared with an elected assembly.
property-based voting: A system in which only people who pay enough tax are allowed to vote. The poor are left out.
girondins: A group of revolutionary deputies, several of whom came from the Gironde (Bordeaux). They wanted war in 1792 but distrusted the people of Paris.
fédéré: A National Guard volunteer who came to Paris from the provinces. The fédérés from Marseille made La Marseillaise famous.
national anthem: A country's official song, played at ceremonies and sports matches. France's is La Marseillaise.
sans-culottes: The revolutionaries from the ordinary people of Paris: craftsmen, shopkeepers, workers. They wore long trousers, not the knee-breeches (culottes) of the nobles.
paris commune: The government of the city of Paris during the Revolution. In August 1792, a very revolutionary new Commune took power at the City Hall.
national convention: The assembly elected in 1792 by all men to write a new constitution. It was the Convention that proclaimed the Republic.
universal suffrage: The right to vote for all adult citizens. In 1792 it only applied to men; French women would only vote in 1945.
montagnards: The most revolutionary deputies in the Convention, like Robespierre, Danton and Marat. They sat on the highest benches, called "the Mountain".
guillotine: A machine for cutting off heads, adopted in 1792. Doctor Guillotin had suggested it so that the death penalty would be the same for everyone and cause less suffering.
infernal columns: Columns of republican soldiers sent to the Vendée in 1794, who burned villages and massacred thousands of inhabitants.
civil war: A war between people of the same country.
committee of public safety: A small group of twelve deputies that ran France in 1793–1794, during the war and the Terror. Robespierre was its most famous member.
martyr: A person who dies for their ideas or their faith, and who is then honoured as a hero.
museum: A place where works of art, old objects or scientific collections are kept and shown to the public.
vandalism: Deliberately destroying works of art, monuments or property. The word was invented during the Revolution by Abbé Grégoire, after the Vandals, a people who sacked Rome.
terror: The period from September 1793 to July 1794 when the revolutionary government had its enemies, real or imagined, arrested and executed.
law of suspects: The law of September 1793 that allowed anyone suspected of being an enemy of the Revolution to be arrested, even without proof.
revolutionary tribunal: The court created in 1793 to try enemies of the Revolution. Its trials were very quick and often ended in death sentences.
republican calendar: The calendar created in 1793 to replace the Christian calendar. Year I began on 22 September 1792, the day the Republic was born.
décade: In the Republican calendar, a ten-day week. The tenth day, décadi, was the day of rest.
slavery: The situation of a person who belongs to someone else, like an object. An enslaved person can be sold and is forced to work without pay.
abolition: Getting rid of a law or a practice. To abolish slavery means to ban it.
dechristianisation: The movement of 1793–1794 that tried to get rid of the Christian religion: churches were closed, bells melted down, and priests forced to give up their work.
incroyables: Fashionable young men under the Directory, with outrageous clothes. They didn't pronounce their "r"s and said "C'est inc'oyable!" ("It's inc'edible!").
assignat: A paper banknote created in 1790, backed by the sale of national properties. The state printed so many that they became almost worthless.
metre: The unit of length created during the Revolution. It was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
metric system: The system of measurement created during the Revolution (metre, litre, gram...), where you go from one unit to the next by multiplying or dividing by 10.
decimal: Counting in tens. In a decimal system, 10 small units make one bigger unit.
royalist: A person who wants a king to lead the country.
directory: The government that ran France from 1795 to 1799, with five Directors and two assemblies.
campo formio: The peace treaty signed in 1797 between France and Austria after Bonaparte's victories in Italy.
propaganda: Messages, pictures and stories spread to convince people and make them think a certain way, sometimes by hiding the truth.
rosetta stone: A carved stone found in Egypt in 1799, with the same text in hieroglyphs, demotic script and Greek. It made it possible to decipher hieroglyphs.
hieroglyphs: The signs of ancient Egyptian writing, which often show an object, an animal or a person.
egyptology: The science that studies the history, language and civilisation of ancient Egypt.
consul: Under the Consulate (1799–1804), one of the three heads of government. The First Consul, Bonaparte, had almost all the power.
coup d'état: Taking power by force or by trickery, without respecting the law. It is French for "a blow against the state".
lycée: A French high school, created by Napoleon in 1802 for older pupils. Lycées still exist today.
military parade: A procession where soldiers march in step, with music, in front of the public and the country's leaders.
liberty, equality, fraternity: The motto of the French Republic (Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité). It was born during the Revolution and is written on town halls and schools.
phrygian cap: A red cap with a floppy point. In ancient times it was worn by freed slaves, so it became the symbol of liberty.
secularism: In France, called laïcité: the principle that the state favours no religion. Everyone is free to believe or not believe, and state schools stay neutral.
universal declaration of human rights: The text adopted by the United Nations in 1948 listing the rights of all human beings, everywhere in the world.
bicentenary: The 200th anniversary of an event. The bicentenary of the French Revolution was celebrated in 1989.
